Inside, the air was a cloying mixture of expensive cigar smoke and the metallic tang of ozone, illuminated only by the flickering, jaundiced glow of overhead lamps that shuddered with every jolt of the tracks. Outside the window, the landscape was a smeared charcoal blur, but inside, the stillness was absolute—until the conductor’s heavy tread stopped abruptly outside Compartment Seven. There, beneath the velvet curtain, a single, gold-rimmed monocle lay shattered on the mahogany floor, reflecting the pale, wide-eyed stare of a man who had died mid-sentence, his frozen finger still pointing toward the locked door.

The Orient Express had become a rattling iron casket, hurtling through the suffocating blackness of the Alps. Inside Carriage Seven, the air was a stale cocktail of expensive cigar smoke, damp wool, and the metallic tang of old brass. The rhythmic *thrum-thrum* of the wheels against the tracks acted as a hypnotic metronome, masking the frantic heartbeat of the passengers huddled in their velvet berths. Outside, the frost clawed at the windowpanes in jagged, crystalline fingers, blurring the moonlight into ghostly smears, while inside, the dim amber glow of the sconces flickered violently with every jolt. It was in this fragile suspension between destinations—somewhere in the void between Zurich and Venice—that the scream finally tore through the silence, sharp and sudden, cutting through the velvet luxury like a razor through silk.

Inside Carriage Seven, the air was a stale cocktail of expensive cigar smoke, damp wool, and the metallic tang of old heaters. In the far corner of the lounge, a single crystal glass of brandy sat abandoned on a velvet settee, still swirling slightly, beside a leather briefcase that had been snapped open with violent haste. Outside, the darkness of the countryside pressed hard against the glass, reflecting not the passing trees, but the pale, wide-eyed face of a man who had realized too late that he was not the only one awake.
